unit.title: JavaScript: making decisions
unit.description: true and false, comparing values, if, else if and else, combining conditions

cards.definition: A value that is either true or false: the answer to a yes or no question.
Compare two values and give true or false: > greater than, < less than, >= at least, <= at most.
Checks that two values are equal AND of the same type, and gives true or false.
Runs a block of code only when a condition is true, and another block otherwise.
Combine conditions: && needs both sides to be true, || needs at least one of them.
cards.example: if (age >= 18 && hasTicket) lets in adults who have a ticket.

cards.definition: Gives true when two values are different, in value or in type.

exercises.explain: A comparison answers a yes or no question with a boolean: true or false.
whyWrong: 8 is greater than 5, so the comparison is true.
A comparison gives true or false, not a number.
> compares; it does not subtract.

exercises.prompt: Which sign checks that two values are equal?
exercises.explain: = stores a value, === compares two values. Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes.
whyWrong: A single = stores a value in a variable; it does not compare.
=> is used to write arrow functions.
!== checks that two values are DIFFERENT.

exercises.explain: if runs its block when the condition is true; else runs when it is false. Exactly one of the two runs.
whyWrong: 20 is at least 18: the condition is true, so the first block runs.
Only one of the two blocks runs, never both.
With an else, one of the two blocks always runs.

exercises.explain: Without else, when the condition is false, the block is simply skipped.
whyWrong: 0 is not greater than 0: the condition is false.
console.log is inside the if block, which does not run.
An if without else is perfectly valid.

exercises.explain: === checks the value AND the type. "5" is a string, 5 is a number: they are not strictly equal.
whyWrong: They look alike, but one is text and the other a number.
A comparison gives true or false.
Comparing two different types is allowed.

exercises.prompt: In if (x = 10), the single = compares x with 10.
exercises.explain: A single = assigns: it puts 10 into x. To compare, write x === 10.
&& (and) is true only when both sides are true. || (or) is true when at least one side is.
whyWrong: && needs BOTH sides to be true, and hasTicket is false.
The result is a boolean here, not the age.
Both variables have values, so nothing is undefined.

exercises.prompt: Build the start of a condition that checks that score is greater than 100.
exercises.explain: if (score > 100) runs its block only when score is above 100.

exercises.prompt: This code prints "Admin" even for a guest. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explain: role = "admin" assigns instead of comparing, and a text that is not empty counts as true. Write role === "admin".
else if adds another test. JavaScript checks the tests from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true.
whyWrong: 15 is not above 25, so the first block is skipped.
15 is above 10: the second test is true, so the else is never reached.
As soon as one test is true, the rest is skipped.

exercises.prompt: Build the start of a condition that checks that age is at least 18.
exercises.explain: if (age >= 18) runs its block when age is 18 or more. >= means at least.
